passage:
Madhav's diary, Thursday night.
Day 9 at the architects' office. Today Mr Sood, the partner, barked, “Who taught you to staple?” in front of eight people, and nobody looked up. Then I photocopied drawings for six hours. I keep wondering whether this is just how it is. I wanted to apologise to everyone, even for breathing. At tea, Afreen didi, the senior architect, sat next to me. She said, “Copying and stapling is what interns do first. But being barked at in front of the team isn't something you should have to swallow. You can ask, 'Could you tell me privately how you want it?' If it keeps happening, tell the intern coordinator and me.” My hands are still a bit shaky. Tomorrow I'll try the sentence.
Madhav

qa.q: How many people were in the room when Mr Sood barked at Madhav?
qa.a: Eight people were there when Mr Sood barked.

qa.q: What was Madhav feeling after the shouting and the six hours of copying?
qa.a: Madhav felt small and unsure whether this was normal, wanting to apologise to everyone even for breathing, and still had shaky hands.

qa.q: What did Afreen say that helped Madhav tell normal from unfair?
qa.a: Afreen said that copying and stapling is what interns do first, but being barked at in front of the team is not something to swallow, and gave a sentence to use and a place to go if it continues.

qa.q: Why might the eight people in the room have kept their eyes down?
qa.a: They may have been unsure how to step in or fearful of the partner, which fits nobody looking up and shows how a rigid hierarchy keeps people quiet.

grounding: An intern is spoken to sharply and given menial work and a mentor helps tell what is normal from what is unfair.

passage:
Harish: bhaiya are you free? rough week at the newspaper office
Bhupen: Tell me.
Harish: the news editor threw a file on my desk and said “my tea, not this rubbish” in front of the whole desk. everyone just kept typing
Bhupen: What had you done?
Harish: fetched tea four times today, then wrote three city briefs, then he said the briefs were rubbish
Bhupen: Tea runs and briefs are normal for an intern. Being shouted at in front of everyone isn't. Did any of the feedback on the briefs concern the actual work?
Harish: he said the second para was buried
Bhupen: That part is useful. The shouting isn't. Ask him next time for feedback in private, and if it repeats, talk to the internship coordinator. I'll come with you if you want.
Harish: ok. I'll feel small tomorrow but I'll try
Bhupen: You're not small. Call me after.

qa.q: How many times had Harish fetched tea that day?
qa.a: Harish had fetched tea four times that day.

qa.q: Why did Harish say, “I'll feel small tomorrow but I'll try”?
qa.a: Harish still feels small after being shouted at in front of the whole desk, yet is willing to try Bhupen's suggestions.

qa.q: What did Bhupen suggest for handling the editor's feedback in future?
qa.a: Bhupen suggested asking the editor for feedback in private and, if the shouting repeats, talking to the internship coordinator, with Bhupen offering to go along.

qa.q: What might Bhupen be thinking when he says, “You're not small”?
qa.a: Bhupen seems to want Harish to stop believing the shouting says something about Harish's worth, and wants to stay close for support.

grounding: An intern is shouted at and given menial work, and a trusted mentor helps the intern tell normal tasks from unfair treatment.

passage: Mentor's note, week two of the internship programme. Uma, our design intern, came to see me after lunch. Hemant, the senior architect she is assigned to, has had her photocopying drawings and fetching his lunch for nine days, and yesterday he snapped, 'Don't speak in client meetings.' She asked me whether this is normal. She looked small and apologetic, as if she were the problem. I told her that photocopying is part of every intern's week, and so is staying quiet in client meetings at first. Fetching lunch and being snapped at are not. I will speak to Hemant about the tone and the lunch, and I've asked the studio head to put Uma on Thursday's site visit with another team. She will check in with me again in a week.

qa.q: How long had Uma been photocopying and fetching lunch?
qa.a: For nine days.

qa.q: How did Uma seem when asking whether this was normal?
qa.a: She seemed small and apologetic, unsure and ashamed, as if she were the problem.

qa.q: How did the mentor help Uma tell normal from unfair?
qa.a: By separating what is normal for interns, like photocopying and staying quiet in client meetings, from what isn't, like fetching lunch and being snapped at, and then acting on it.

qa.q: How might Hemant see his treatment of Uma?
qa.a: He may see it as the usual way seniors treat interns, without noticing that the lunch errands and sharp tone cross a line.

grounding: A mentor's note shows an intern unsure if sharp treatment is normal, and the mentor helping separate the normal from the unfair.

passage:
Journal, Wednesday.
Day eight at the newspaper. Asif sir, the night editor, pushed my story back across the desk today and said, 'Is this English or soup?' in front of the whole desk. Nobody looked up. I retyped it three times. Then he sent me to get tea for six people, then to count old papers in the store.
Is this how journalism works? Everyone keeps saying 'this is how we all started'. I keep saying 'yes sir, sorry sir' to everything, even when I don't know what I'm sorry for.
At seven, Meenakshi di from the features desk stopped me by the lift. 'The soup comment was out of line. Tea runs are normal here; the shouting isn't. Sit with me tomorrow and I'll show you how to edit.'
I cried a little on the bus. Good crying, I think.
Gurpreet

qa.q: What did Asif sir say when pushing the story back?
qa.a: 'Is this English or soup?'

qa.q: Why does Gurpreet keep saying 'yes sir, sorry sir'?
qa.a: Gurpreet feels small and anxious, trying to please even without knowing what the apology is for.

qa.q: How did Meenakshi di help Gurpreet?
qa.a: She separated what is normal, like tea runs, from what isn't, like the shouting, and offered to teach editing the next day.

qa.q: What might the rest of the desk be thinking when nobody looks up?
qa.a: They may see the sharpness as ordinary, the way they 'all started', or feel uneasy but unwilling to challenge the night editor.

grounding: An intern spoken to sharply and given menial work wonders if it is normal, and a senior colleague helps tell the difference.

Sangeeta: chef shouted 'move, useless' at me today in front of the whole line. and I've been peeling onions for 3 days. is that normal in hotel kitchens?
Jomon: onions for 3 days, yes, sadly normal. every trainee peels. I did 2 weeks of potatoes 😅
Jomon: the 'useless' part, not ok. shouting 'move' in a rush happens. name-calling shouldn't
Sangeeta: I said sorry chef like 5 times
Sangeeta: I just want him to like me
Jomon: makes sense. but you don't need to apologise for being in the way during a rush. just say 'yes chef' and move
Jomon: if the name-calling keeps happening, tell the sous chef or me, and we'll raise it with HR
Sangeeta: ok. thank you 🙏
Jomon: you're doing fine. onion speed is a real skill 🙂

qa.a: For 3 days.

qa.q: What does 'I just want him to like me' show about Sangeeta?
qa.a: Sangeeta feels small and anxious to please, apologising again and again to win the chef's approval.

qa.q: What did Jomon advise about the name-calling?
qa.a: To tell the sous chef or Jomon if it keeps happening, so it can be raised with HR.

passage: At the tehsil office in Hoshiarpur, Ankita's internship had become photocopying. Three weeks of it. On Thursday the head clerk, Mr Bedi, tossed a file onto her desk. "Two hundred copies. And don't stand there like a statue." The peon looked away. The other intern, Rupinder, kept his head down and hurried past. Ankita stapled until her thumb ached, wondering whether this was simply how offices worked or whether she was being punished for something. That evening she heard herself say, "I'll come early tomorrow, sir, anything you need," and hated how small her voice sounded. Jasleen, the junior officer who had signed her internship form, found her at the tea stall. "Copying is normal for interns," Jasleen said. "Being barked at is not. Keep a note of what you're asked to do. And on Monday, you're coming on my site visit."

qa.q: How many copies did Mr Bedi ask for?
qa.a: He asked for two hundred copies.

qa.q: What was Ankita feeling when she offered to come early?
qa.a: She felt small and anxious to please, unsure whether she was being punished, and hated how her voice sounded.

qa.q: How did Jasleen help Ankita tell normal from unfair?
qa.a: Jasleen separated the two plainly, copying is normal but being barked at is not, and gave practical steps: note the tasks and join the site visit.

qa.q: What might Rupinder be going through as he keeps his head down?
qa.a: Rupinder may feel the same fear and choose silence to stay safe, which makes the sharp tone look normal to everyone.

grounding: Shows an intern given menial work and spoken to sharply, unsure what is normal, until a trusted mentor helps her tell the difference.
